title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde
setting: London, from a Mayfair studio to the docks, over roughly eighteen years
lengthNote: A preface and twenty chapters, of which one contains almost no action at all
openingLine: The studio was filled with the rich odour of roses, and when the light summer wind stirred amidst the trees of the garden, there came through the open door the heavy scent of the lilac, or the more delicate perfume of the pink-flowering thorn.
summary: A painter finishes the best thing he will ever do, a clever man says something careless about youth in front of the sitter, and the sitter wishes the picture could age instead of him. Wilde then spends twenty chapters watching what a person becomes when consequences are stored somewhere else. The talk is the pleasure of the book and also its subject: almost every disaster in it starts with a remark made to be admired.
referenceStyle: chapter, with the 1891 opening cited as Preface

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Picture of Dorian Gray — Wilde’s revised 1891 edition
sourceText.note: Wilde’s only novel exists in two authorial forms. This is the twenty-chapter book of 1891 with its preface, not the thirteen-chapter version printed in Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine in 1890.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: In Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine, in thirteen chapters, and attacked in the press within days.

atAGlance.label: Revised
atAGlance.note: Wilde added six chapters, softened some passages, sharpened others, and put a preface of aphorisms in front of the whole thing.

atAGlance.label: Text used here
atAGlance.note: Twenty chapters and a preface, published in London by Ward, Lock and Co.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Chapter XI covers eighteen years and contains scarcely a scene — a catalogue of jewels, embroideries and ancestors standing in for a life.

structure.label: Chapters I-II
structure.title: A portrait, a conversation and a wish
structure.summary: Basil Hallward will not exhibit his best painting because he has put too much of himself into it. Lord Henry meets the sitter anyway and spends an afternoon in a garden explaining that youth is the only thing worth having. By the end of the second chapter Dorian has wished the picture would take the years instead, and Basil’s studio has produced two things it cannot control.

scenes.summary: Basil explains to Lord Henry why the portrait can never be shown; Dorian is announced.
The sermon in the garden, the finished picture, the wish, and Basil offering to destroy the canvas.

structure.label: Chapters III-VIII
structure.title: An actress who stops being able to act
structure.summary: Dorian falls in love with a girl who plays Juliet in a shabby theatre off the Euston Road, and loves her for the parts rather than the person. When love makes her performance sincere and therefore bad, he tells her so in front of her mother and leaves. She kills herself that night, and the mouth of the portrait has changed by morning.

scenes.summary: Lord Henry’s inquiries into Dorian’s parentage; the engagement announced over tea.
The Vanes at home: a mother acting grief, a brother leaving for Australia and a sworn threat.
Sibyl plays badly because she has stopped pretending; Dorian’s speech in the dressing room; a cruel line added to the painted mouth.
The news of her death arrives with the morning post, and Lord Henry converts it into an aesthetic experience over lunch.

structure.label: Chapters IX-XI
structure.title: The picture goes upstairs and eighteen years go past
structure.summary: Dorian has the canvas carried to the disused schoolroom at the top of the house, locks it in and keeps the key. A yellow-bound French novel arrives from Lord Henry, and the narrative loosens into years of collecting — perfumes, jewels, embroideries, portraits of ancestors — with rumours accumulating in the gaps between paragraphs.

scenes.summary: Basil calls to console him, is refused a sight of the portrait, and is refused a drawing of Sibyl.
The frame-maker’s men carry the picture upstairs; the book in the yellow paper cover arrives.
Eighteen years of study, fashion, ritual and rumour, told almost entirely as inventory.

structure.label: Chapters XII-XIV
structure.title: The painter asks to see his own work
structure.summary: Basil comes on the eve of his thirty-eighth birthday to repeat the rumours to his face and to ask him to deny them. Dorian takes him up to the schoolroom instead, shows him the thing he made, and stabs him behind the ear. The next morning a chemist he once knew is blackmailed into destroying the body.

scenes.summary: A meeting in the fog at Grosvenor Square; Basil lists the friends Dorian has ruined.
The lamp held up to the portrait, the prayer, and the knife on the chest behind the door.
A forged note, Alan Campbell’s arrival, and five hours in a locked room with nitric acid.

structure.label: Chapters XV-XVIII
structure.title: A sailor with a long memory, and a shot in a beech wood
structure.summary: Dorian goes from a dinner party to an opium den near the docks, where a woman calls him Prince Charming and Sibyl’s brother hears it. James Vane holds a pistol to his head, is talked out of it by a face that looks twenty, and follows him to the country. A beater’s accident removes the threat and leaves Dorian more frightened than before.

scenes.summary: Lady Narborough’s dinner, then Blue Gate Fields; the woman’s name for him nearly kills him.
Selby Royal, an argument about naming things, and a face at the conservatory window.
Three days indoors, a shooting party, and a body brought in from the covert.

structure.label: Chapters XIX-XX
structure.title: An attempt at goodness, and a knife
structure.summary: Dorian tells Lord Henry he intends to reform and offers a spared country girl as evidence; Lord Henry laughs and denies that a book can poison anybody. Alone that night, Dorian looks for a change in the picture, finds only cunning added to the face, and attacks the canvas with the knife that killed Basil.

scenes.summary: The last conversation: confession offered as a story and refused as impossible.
A walk home, a mirror broken, the portrait unchanged, and a cry heard by the servants.

characters.name: Dorian Gray
characters.role: A young man of fortune with an unusually beautiful face
characters.summary: He is nineteen, orphaned, rich and almost characterless when the book starts, which is exactly why Lord Henry can write on him. What he acquires over eighteen years is not wickedness so much as the habit of treating other people as experiences, and the one thing the novel never lets him have is a consequence he can see.
characters.clue: He is nineteen when a painter finishes him and a lord explains him, and eighteen years later he still looks it.

characters.name: Lord Henry Wotton
characters.role: A titled talker with no occupation
characters.summary: He supplies the theory, takes none of the risk, and is the only major character alive and unmarked at the end. His paradoxes are designed to be quoted rather than acted on, and the novel’s quiet joke is that the one person who lives by them is the one person Lord Henry never expected to be listened to by.
characters.clue: He never does anything in the whole book except talk, and everything that happens in it can be traced to something he said in a garden.

characters.name: Basil Hallward
characters.summary: He refuses to exhibit the picture because it shows the feeling of the man who made it rather than the face of the man who sat for it, which is the most honest statement about art in the book. His worship is genuine and useless: he is the only person who tries to ask Dorian a direct moral question, and he is killed for it.
characters.clue: He paints the best thing he will ever do and will not show it to anyone, because it is a portrait of his own feeling rather than of a face.

characters.name: Sibyl Vane
characters.role: An actress at a small theatre off the Euston Road
characters.summary: She plays Juliet, Rosalind and Imogen for a shilling audience, and Dorian loves the succession of heroines rather than the girl performing them. When real feeling makes her a bad actress she becomes worthless to him, and the novel’s sharpest irony is that her sincerity is what he punishes.
characters.clue: She is loved for playing Juliet and Rosalind, and abandoned the night she stops being able to pretend.

characters.name: James Vane
characters.summary: He leaves for Australia swearing to kill the gentleman if anything happens to his sister, and returns years later as the one force in the novel that cannot be talked round. He is beaten by the same thing that has protected Dorian throughout — a face too young to belong to the man he is looking for.
characters.clue: He swears an oath on a dreary road before sailing, and comes back eighteen years later to find that the man he wants still looks like a boy.

characters.name: Alan Campbell
characters.role: A chemist, once an intimate friend
characters.summary: He arrives certain that nothing will make him help and leaves having agreed, after Dorian writes a single sentence on a piece of paper. Wilde never says what the sentence contains, and the blank is the most efficient thing in the novel: a reader is handed the mechanics of blackmail without a word of its content.
characters.clue: A scientist who swears he will do nothing, reads one written line, and spends five hours upstairs with a set of chemicals.

characters.name: The portrait
characters.role: Basil’s canvas, kept behind a locked door
characters.summary: It changes first at the mouth, then the hands, then the whole visage, and Dorian visits it the way other people visit a conscience. It is the only character in the novel that keeps an accurate record, and the last two pages establish that it was also the only one telling the truth about what he looked like.
characters.clue: It hangs behind a locked schoolroom door under a Venetian cloth, and it is the only honest record of a man in the whole book.

themes.name: Beauty and surface
themes.summary: The preface announces that those who go beneath the surface do so at their peril, and the plot then buries the truth under a cloth in a locked room. Everyone in the novel makes moral judgements from faces, and everyone is wrong. The book is not an argument that appearances deceive; it is an argument that people would rather they did.
themes.development: A face admired in a studio, a mouth that changes overnight, a murder prevented by looking twenty, and a body identified only by its rings.

themes.name: Influence
themes.summary: Lord Henry claims that all influence is immoral because it stops a person being themselves, and immediately sets about influencing a nineteen-year-old. The novel takes him seriously enough to test the claim: Dorian’s whole life afterwards is an echo of somebody else’s music, which is the objection Lord Henry himself raised.
themes.development: A sermon in a garden in Chapter II, a book sent as a present in Chapter X, and a final conversation in which the teacher denies that anything he said could have had an effect.

themes.name: Art and morality
themes.summary: The preface insists that a book cannot be moral or immoral and that art has no ethical sympathies. The plot then hands Dorian a novel that changes his life and a painting that keeps his moral accounts. Wilde builds a story whose events contradict its own opening statement, and never resolves the disagreement.
themes.development: Aphorisms in the preface, a yellow book in Chapter X, a man poisoned by it in Chapter XI, and Lord Henry’s flat denial in Chapter XIX that such a thing is possible.

themes.name: The double life
themes.summary: Dorian goes from a Mayfair dinner to a den near the docks in the same evening and is received in both. The doubling is spatial as much as moral — a house with a locked upper room, a city with a respectable west and an unwatched east — and he describes the arrangement itself as a pleasure.
themes.development: A locked schoolroom in Chapter X, the calm demeanour noted in Chapter XV, and a country house where the hunted man is a guest with a headache.

themes.name: Youth and time
themes.summary: Lord Henry’s opening speech is about the shortness of youth, and Dorian’s wish is a refusal to be billed for time passing. What the novel shows is that the time still happens: eighteen years go by in one chapter of catalogues, and the man who stopped ageing has also stopped accumulating a life.
themes.development: A warning in a garden, a wish beside an easel, an inventory in Chapter XI, and a dead man of fifty found in evening dress.

themes.name: Conscience and confession
themes.summary: Dorian keeps trying to confess and keeps being prevented — by Lord Henry’s amusement, by Basil’s death, by his own vanity about how the story will sound. The portrait offers him an exact account of himself at any hour, which is what a conscience is, and he responds by locking it upstairs and visiting when the mood takes him.
themes.development: A prayer in front of the canvas in Chapter XIII, a confession offered as gossip in Chapter XIX, and a last look for improvement that finds only cunning.

techniques.name: Epigram and paradox
techniques.definition: A short, polished statement that inverts an expected idea in order to be memorable.
techniques.inThisBook: Lord Henry speaks almost entirely in them, and the novel’s method is to let a line that works brilliantly in a drawing room be acted on by somebody who takes it literally.

techniques.name: The portrait as symbol
techniques.definition: An object made to carry the meaning that characters cannot state directly.
techniques.inThisBook: The canvas keeps the record: cruelty at the mouth, blood on the hands, cunning in the eyes. It is a conscience with a frame, and it is the only thing in the book Dorian cannot argue with.

techniques.name: The Faustian pact
techniques.definition: A bargain in which something is granted at a price the taker does not fully understand.
techniques.inThisBook: Wilde gives no devil, no contract and no witness — only a wish said aloud in a studio, which is granted and then never explained by anybody.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: A long list of objects or names used in place of narrative.
techniques.inThisBook: Chapter XI replaces eighteen years with embroideries, jewels, church vestments and Dorian’s ancestors. The absence of scenes is the point: a life spent collecting leaves nothing that can be told as a story.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Third-person narration that slips into a character’s own vocabulary and self-justification.
techniques.inThisBook: The prose keeps taking Dorian’s side from inside his head, so that a reader has to notice for themselves when the language of exquisite sensation is describing something squalid.

techniques.name: Aestheticist description
techniques.definition: Dense, sensuous writing about surfaces, colours, scents and materials.
techniques.inThisBook: The novel opens on roses, lilac and thorn before a person is mentioned, and it returns to perfumes and fabrics whenever the moral pressure rises — the style itself is a way of looking away.

quotations.text: There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written, or badly written. That is all.
quotations.context: From the preface Wilde added in 1891, after the reviews of the magazine version.
quotations.analysis: This is a reply to specific attacks, printed as if it were a general principle. Set it against Chapter XI, where a book poisons the hero, and against Lord Henry’s denial in Chapter XIX that such a thing could happen: the preface and the plot are arguing with each other on the same pages.

quotations.text: All art is at once surface and symbol. Those who go beneath the surface do so at their peril. Those who read the symbol do so at their peril.
quotations.context: The preface’s last substantial pair of statements before the closing line.
quotations.analysis: The two sentences are identical in shape and cancel each other, which leaves a reader with no safe position from which to interpret. It is also a plot summary: this is a book in which a surface and a symbol are separated from each other, and everyone who looks under the cloth comes off badly.

quotations.text: All art is quite useless.
quotations.context: The final line of the preface, standing alone.
quotations.analysis: Useless here means unable to be put to work, which was the aesthetic movement’s defence against a century that wanted everything to improve somebody. The book that follows is about a work of art doing a job — keeping accounts — and destroying the man it belongs to.

quotations.text: I know you will laugh at me,” he replied, “but I really can’t exhibit it. I have put too much of myself into it.
quotations.speaker: Basil Hallward
quotations.context: Basil explaining why the finished portrait will never be shown.
quotations.analysis: He thinks he is confessing to bad art and he is confessing to love. The line also sets the novel’s central proposition before any magic happens: a portrait can contain a person who is not the sitter, which is what makes the later transfer feel less like a spell than a completion.

quotations.text: But beauty, real beauty, ends where an intellectual expression begins.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Lord Henry, in the studio, before he has met Dorian.
quotations.analysis: It is said as a joke about clever men’s faces and it is the rule Dorian will live by: to remain beautiful is to remain unmarked by thought. The novel then arranges for a face that never records a thought and a canvas that records every one, and lets the reader decide which is the man.

quotations.text: I have grown to love secrecy. It seems to be the one thing that can make modern life mysterious or marvellous to us. The commonest thing is delightful if one only hides it.
quotations.speaker: Basil Hallward
quotations.context: Basil explaining why he has never told anyone Dorian’s name.
quotations.analysis: The novel’s great theme is stated in the first chapter by the man who will be murdered for wanting things brought into the open. Concealment is presented here as a refinement of pleasure rather than a moral failure, which is the exact argument Dorian will later use about a locked room at the top of a house.

quotations.text: There is no such thing as a good influence, Mr. Gray. All influence is immoral⁠—immoral from the scientific point of view.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: The opening of the speech in the garden, minutes after being introduced.
quotations.analysis: He is establishing his authority by disclaiming it, which is the oldest move a persuader has. From the scientific point of view is decoration — there is no science in the sentence — and the whole novel is the experiment that follows from a man announcing that influence is impossible and then applying it for an hour.

quotations.text: The aim of life is self-development. To realize one’s nature perfectly⁠—that is what each of us is here for.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: The same speech, a few sentences on.
quotations.analysis: It is genuinely liberating and completely unsupervised: a doctrine with no account at all of other people. Wilde gives it to a man who will never test it, and then hands the testing to somebody with money, beauty and eighteen years, which is as close as the novel comes to an argument against its own best lines.

quotations.text: The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Part of the garden speech, arguing that resistance is what makes desire monstrous.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning around it is medical rather than moral — the body sins once and has done with its sin — and that is the trick. A sentence built to sound like a cure for obsession is in fact a licence, and the novel spends twenty chapters showing that yielding does not get rid of anything.

quotations.text: Nothing can cure the soul but the senses, just as nothing can cure the senses but the soul.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Said quietly, with a hand on Dorian’s shoulder, in the garden.
quotations.analysis: Dorian repeats this line to himself sixteen chapters later on the way to an opium den, and Wilde prints it twice in that scene to make sure the reader hears where it has ended up. A balanced, harmless-sounding chiasmus becomes a man’s excuse for buying oblivion the night after a murder.

quotations.text: If it were I who was to be always young, and the picture that was to grow old! For that⁠—for that⁠—I would give everything! Yes, there is nothing in the whole world I would not give! I would give my soul for that!
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: In front of the finished portrait, after Lord Henry’s speech in the garden.
quotations.analysis: There is no devil, no contract and no witness who understands what has happened: the most consequential sentence in the novel is a tantrum in front of a canvas. Wilde keeps the machinery invisible for the rest of the book, so that a reader can never quite decide whether anything supernatural has occurred or whether Dorian is simply right about himself.

quotations.text: It is the real Dorian Gray⁠—that is all.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Dismissing Dorian’s outburst as merely the young man showing his true character.
quotations.analysis: He means it as a shrug about temperament, and it turns out to be a literal description of the object on the easel. This is the novel’s method in one line: a piece of drawing-room cleverness is quietly promoted into a fact, and nobody in the room notices it happen.

quotations.text: Harry! Sibyl Vane is sacred!
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: Answering Lord Henry’s amused questions about when he will be paying for her.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation marks are the only ones Dorian earns in the whole book, and three chapters later he tells the same girl she has killed his love. Sacred belongs to the vocabulary of worship rather than of affection, which is the flaw: he has cast her as a shrine, and shrines are not allowed to have a bad night.

quotations.text: Yes, Dorian, you will always be fond of me. I represent to you all the sins you have never had the courage to commit.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: At dinner, hours before Sibyl’s performance.
quotations.analysis: He is boasting about being a spectator, and he has the relation exactly backwards — Dorian will commit the sins and Lord Henry will hear about them as anecdotes. The line reads as flirtation on the night it is spoken and as an epitaph by Chapter XX, when the one man who acted is dead and the one who talked is unchanged.

quotations.text: you have killed my love. You used to stir my imagination. Now you don’t even stir my curiosity. You simply produce no effect.
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: In the dressing room, after Sibyl has acted Juliet badly for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The three sentences descend from love to imagination to curiosity to effect, ending in the language of a critic rather than a lover. She has just told him that she can no longer act because she has discovered what love is; he replies by explaining that she was only ever a performance he enjoyed.

quotations.text: It was a poisonous book. The heavy odour of incense seemed to cling about its pages and to trouble the brain.
quotations.context: Dorian reads the yellow-backed French novel Lord Henry has sent him.
quotations.analysis: The narration takes Dorian’s side of the argument the preface has just refused: a book here is an atmosphere you breathe rather than a set of propositions you weigh. Wilde never names the novel, which leaves it as a pure idea of a dangerous book — and keeps the preface’s denial technically intact.

quotations.text: Dorian Gray had been poisoned by a book.
quotations.context: In the middle of a paragraph about Renaissance methods of murder.
quotations.analysis: It arrives at the end of a list of poisoned helmets, gloves and pomanders, so the book is filed as one more elegant instrument. Seven words flatly contradict the preface, and the novel simply lets both stand — which is either Wilde’s carelessness or the point of publishing the preface at all.

quotations.text: It is the face of my soul.
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: Holding the lamp up to the portrait for Basil, minutes before the murder.
quotations.analysis: He has been asked to deny the rumours and instead produces a physical exhibit, which is a confession made in the only terms he still understands. Basil’s response is to suggest that they pray, and Dorian’s is to reach for a knife — the novel refuses him the one moment in which saying the true thing might have changed anything.

quotations.text: Each of us has heaven and hell in him, Basil
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: In the schoolroom, when Basil urges him to pray.
quotations.analysis: It is said with a wild gesture of despair and it is the most ordinary piece of theology in the novel — the one thing Dorian says that Lord Henry could not have taught him. Within a page he has stabbed the man he said it to, which is the book’s way of showing that knowing the doctrine is not the same as having a conscience.

quotations.text: What was that loathsome red dew that gleamed, wet and glistening, on one of the hands, as though the canvas had sweated blood?
quotations.context: The morning after the murder, looking at the portrait before Alan Campbell arrives.
quotations.analysis: Dew is a word for something clean, and the sentence spends three modifiers being beautiful before it says blood. This is the aestheticist prose doing its usual job of looking away, and the detail it will not name outright is the one that has moved from the body downstairs onto a painted hand.

quotations.text: He himself could not help wondering at the calm of his demeanour, and for a moment felt keenly the terrible pleasure of a double life.
quotations.context: At Lady Narborough’s dinner table, the evening after the body has been destroyed.
quotations.analysis: Terrible pleasure is not remorse; it is connoisseurship applied to his own situation. The novel has him admire his own composure from the outside, which is what the portrait does for him structurally — and it explains why he keeps the thing rather than burning it.

quotations.text: The soul is a terrible reality. It can be bought, and sold, and bartered away. It can be poisoned, or made perfect.
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: The last conversation with Lord Henry, who has just called the soul a fashionable myth.
quotations.analysis: The pupil corrects the teacher, using the commercial verbs Lord Henry taught him, and Lord Henry laughs. This is the only time anyone in the novel states the plot as a fact to somebody who could still act on it, and it is received as a good remark and nothing else.

quotations.text: You are the type of what the age is searching for, and what it is afraid it has found.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Praising Dorian for having produced nothing but himself.
quotations.analysis: Afraid it has found is the sharpest thing Lord Henry says, and he says it without noticing. He has spent the novel recommending a life made entirely of sensation, and here he admits that the age which wants such a life is also frightened of the person who actually lives one.

quotations.text: As it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work, and all that that meant. It would kill the past, and when that was dead, he would be free.
quotations.context: Picking up the knife in front of the portrait on the last night.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is stated as free indirect thought, so the reader gets Dorian’s logic without a narrator to correct it, and the logic is good — except that he has never worked out which of the two of them is the painting. Kill the past is the wish from Chapter II repeated in the language of a man who has run out of other ideas.

quotations.text: Lying on the floor was a dead man, in evening dress, with a knife in his heart. He was withered, wrinkled, and loathsome of visage. It was not till they had examined the rings that they recognized who it was.
quotations.context: The servants break into the locked room; the last sentences of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The book ends with an identification made from jewellery, because the face — the thing everyone in twenty chapters has judged him by — is no longer evidence of anything. Evening dress is the detail that finishes it: the accounts are settled at last, and he is still dressed for dinner.

timeline.label: Oscar Wilde is born in Dublin
timeline.detail: Son of a surgeon and of the poet who wrote as Speranza.

timeline.label: Walter Pater’s Studies in the History of the Renaissance
timeline.detail: Its conclusion — to burn always with a hard, gem-like flame — is the argument Lord Henry repeats in a garden with the ethics removed.

timeline.label: Huysmans publishes A rebours
timeline.detail: The decadent French novel usually identified with the yellow-backed book Lord Henry sends; Wilde declined to confirm it.

timeline.label: The novel appears in Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine
timeline.detail: Thirteen chapters, printed in the July issue, and denounced in several London papers as a book for outlawed noblemen.

timeline.label: The revised book edition
timeline.detail: Published by Ward, Lock and Co. with six new chapters, a preface of aphorisms, and the James Vane plot added to give the second half a pursuer.

timeline.label: Wilde publishes Intentions and Lord Arthur Savile’s Crime
timeline.detail: Wilde’s most productive year as a prose writer, immediately before he turned to the stage.

timeline.label: The Importance of Being Earnest opens at the St James’s Theatre
timeline.detail: In February, with Wilde at the height of his fame and three months from the first trial.

timeline.label: The novel is used as evidence in court
timeline.detail: Passages were read out and Wilde was cross-examined on them during the libel action he brought against the Marquess of Queensberry.

timeline.label: De Profundis is written in Reading Gaol
timeline.detail: A long letter to Lord Alfred Douglas, and Wilde’s own account of a life lived for sensation.

timeline.label: Wilde dies in Paris
timeline.detail: At the Hôtel d’Alsace, aged forty-six, three years after his release.

timeline.label: Albert Lewin’s film for MGM
timeline.detail: Shot in black and white with the portrait revealed in colour — the best-known of many attempts to show what Wilde only describes.

places.name: Grosvenor Square, Mayfair
places.note: Dorian’s house, with the locked schoolroom at the top of it.

places.name: Curzon Street
places.note: Lord Henry’s address, where he is nearly always at home at five o’clock.

places.name: Euston Road
places.note: The Vanes’ shabby lodgings, and the theatre district where Sibyl plays Juliet for a shilling audience.

places.name: Covent Garden
places.note: Where Dorian walks at dawn after leaving Sibyl, among carts of lilies.

places.name: Blue Gate Fields, Shadwell
places.note: The docks district of the opium dens, where a woman calls him Prince Charming and Sibyl’s brother hears it.

places.name: Paris
places.note: Basil’s destination on the night he is killed, and the city of the yellow book and of Wilde’s last years.

criticalViews.position: A Gothic fable with a moral
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading, and the one Wilde himself offered when defending the book: every excess is punished, and the ending delivers exactly the judgement a Victorian reader would want.
criticalViews.counter: The punishment arrives only in the last two pages, after eighteen years of unbroken pleasure, and Lord Henry, whose ideas they were, is never touched at all.

criticalViews.position: A manifesto for aestheticism, and a test of it
criticalViews.summary: The preface states the case for art without ethical sympathies; the novel then puts that case into the hands of a man with money and a beautiful face. It can be read as Wilde arguing with his own position at full strength on both sides.
criticalViews.counter: A reader can reasonably say the argument is rigged, since the aesthetic life is represented almost entirely by furnishings and dinner parties.

criticalViews.summary: Basil’s confession that he has put too much of himself into the picture, the unspecified ruin of a series of young men, and Wilde’s own revisions between 1890 and 1891 have made this the dominant modern reading. The 1891 text is measurably more cautious than the magazine version.
criticalViews.counter: The novel’s own vagueness about what Dorian does can carry many meanings, and reducing it to one risks flattening the social range of the rumours Basil actually lists.

criticalViews.position: A novel about celebrity and surface
criticalViews.summary: Dorian’s fame rests on nothing but how he looks; his influence spreads through imitation of his clothes and manner; and he is finally identified by his rings. Read this way, the book is about a person who is entirely an image and knows it.
criticalViews.counter: It underplays the portrait, which is the one thing in the novel insisting that there is an inside for the surface to conceal.

essayQuestions.question: Who is responsible for what Dorian becomes?
essayQuestions.focus: Influence, agency and Lord Henry’s position
plan: Begin with Lord Henry’s own claim that all influence is immoral, and what he does immediately afterwards.
Use Chapter II to show a nineteen-year-old with no formed character being given one in an afternoon.
Turn the argument at Sibyl’s death, which is Dorian’s decision and Lord Henry’s interpretation.
Weigh the yellow book against Lord Henry’s denial in Chapter XIX that a book can affect anybody.
Close on the last chapter, where the attempt at reform fails because Dorian is still performing for an audience.

essayQuestions.question: How does the portrait work as a symbol?
essayQuestions.focus: The canvas, conscience and what the novel makes visible
plan: Establish Basil’s claim in Chapter I that the picture contains the painter rather than the sitter.
Trace the changes in order — mouth, then hands, then the whole visage — and what each one follows.
Read Chapter XIII as the only confession in the book, made by exhibit rather than in words.
Consider the room: a schoolroom, locked, at the top of the house, visited when the mood takes him.
Conclude with the reversal of the last page and what it implies about where the man was all along.

essayQuestions.question: ’The preface and the plot contradict each other.’ Discuss.
plan: Set out the preface’s claims: no moral or immoral books, no ethical sympathies, all art quite useless.
Put beside them the yellow book in Chapters X and XI, and the flat sentence that Dorian was poisoned by it.
Consider the circumstances: the preface was written in answer to reviews of the 1890 version.
Test whether the contradiction is a failure or a deliberate refusal to settle.
Decide what the ending implies, given that it delivers precisely the moral judgement the preface disowns.

essayQuestions.question: What is the effect of Chapter XI?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, catalogue and the passing of eighteen years
plan: Describe what the chapter contains: perfumes, music, jewels, embroideries, vestments, ancestors, and almost no events.
Ask what is achieved by spending a chapter on objects at the point where a life should be narrated.
Connect the inventory to Dorian’s habit of treating people as experiences to be collected.
Note where the rumours are placed — between the lists, unattributed and never confirmed.
Weigh the cost: many readers find the chapter inert, and the second half has to work harder because of it.

discussionQuestions: Lord Henry never does anything, and is the only major character unharmed at the end. Is that a failure of justice or the point?
Sibyl becomes a bad actress because she has started to feel something real. What is Wilde saying about art and sincerity?
Wilde never tells us what is in the yellow book, or what Dorian writes on the paper that makes Alan Campbell comply. What do those blanks achieve?
Dorian’s last act is meant to be a reform. Is there any point in the novel where reform was genuinely available to him?
Would you print the preface if you were editing the novel today, knowing it was written in answer to hostile reviews?

related.why: The same decade’s other story of a respectable Londoner with a second life and a locked room, and the same refusal to specify the pleasures.
Wilde four years later, using the double life for comedy instead — Bunbury is the same arrangement with nothing at stake.
Published six years afterwards, and the other 1890s novel in which a beautiful surface conceals something that must be dealt with in a sealed room.
The earlier study of a maker destroyed by what he has brought into being, and of a creation that outlives its creator.
James’s novella of the same period, built on the same principle that what is never named is more disturbing than what is described.
